summary: Defines the Extensible Authentication Protocol for PPP, which lets PPP links use many authentication methods before network traffic is sent. It was replaced by RFC 3748.

plainLanguage.summary: Point-to-Point Protocol has an optional step where the two ends prove who they are before any network traffic flows. This RFC defines the mechanism for that step, EAP. It does not say how to check an identity. Instead it says how to ask questions, how to answer them, and how to finish with a yes or no, so that a password check, a one-time code or a token card can all be plugged in.

what are the eap packet codes

subtitle: A PPP authentication protocol that leaves the choice of how to prove identity until the moment it is needed.

tldr.problem: PPP negotiates an authentication protocol when the link is set up, which means a server that only forwards traffic to a back-end server cannot use a mechanism it does not itself understand.
tldr.mechanism: EAP defers the choice of mechanism until the authentication phase. The authenticator sends requests, the peer answers, and the exchange ends with a success or failure packet, so new authentication methods can be added without changing PPP.
tldr.outcome: Any number of mechanisms can be carried inside the same exchange, including token cards and one-time passwords. RFC 2284 was obsoleted by RFC 3748.

facts.label: EAP types
facts.value: 1 Identity, 2 Notification, 3 Nak, 4 MD5-Challenge, 5 OTP, 6 Token Card

today: RFC 2284 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 3748. It was updated by RFC 2484.

sections.title: Why PPP Needs EAP
sections.content:
To establish communications over a point-to-point link, each end of the PPP link must first send LCP packets to configure the data link during the Link Establishment phase. After the link has been established, PPP provides for an optional Authentication phase before proceeding to the Network-Layer Protocol phase.

By default authentication is not mandatory. If authentication of the link is desired, an implementation MUST specify the Authentication-Protocol Configuration Option during Link Establishment phase. These authentication protocols are intended for use primarily by hosts and routers that connect to a PPP network server over switched circuits or dial-up lines, but might be applied to dedicated links as well. The server can use the identification of the connecting host or router in the selection of options for network layer negotiations.

The document defines several terms. The authenticator is the end of the link requiring the authentication, and it specifies the authentication protocol to be used in the Configure-Request during Link Establishment phase. The peer is the other end of the link, the end being authenticated. To silently discard means to throw the packet away without further processing, though the implementation SHOULD be able to log the error, including the contents of the discarded packet, and SHOULD record the event in a statistics counter. A displayable message is a human readable string of characters that MUST NOT affect operation of the protocol, and whose encoding MUST follow the UTF-8 transformation format.
sections.plainLanguage: A PPP link is set up in stages. First the two ends negotiate the link itself, then, if the network operator wants it, they authenticate, and only then does normal network traffic start. The side that checks the identity is the authenticator; the side being checked is the peer.

sections.title: How EAP Works
sections.content:
EAP is a general protocol for PPP authentication which supports multiple authentication mechanisms. It does not select a specific mechanism at Link Control Phase, but postpones the choice until the Authentication Phase. This allows the authenticator to request more information before determining the specific mechanism, and it permits the use of a back-end server that actually implements the various mechanisms while the PPP authenticator merely passes through the authentication exchange.

The exchange has three steps. After the Link Establishment phase is complete, the authenticator sends one or more Requests to authenticate the peer, each with a type field indicating what is being requested, such as Identity, an MD5 challenge, One-Time Passwords or Generic Token Card. The MD5-challenge type corresponds closely to the CHAP authentication protocol. Typically the authenticator sends an initial Identity Request followed by one or more Requests for authentication information, but an initial Identity Request is not required and may be bypassed where the identity is presumed, as on leased lines or dedicated dial-ups.

The peer sends a Response packet in reply to each Request, with a type field corresponding to that of the Request. The authenticator ends the authentication phase with a Success or a Failure packet.

The RFC sets out the advantages and the disadvantages. EAP can support multiple authentication mechanisms without pre-negotiating one during the LCP phase, and a device that does not need to understand each request type, such as a network access server, can act as a passthrough agent for a back-end server on a host, looking only for the success or failure code to end the authentication phase. The disadvantages are that EAP requires the addition of a new authentication type to LCP, so PPP implementations must be modified to use it, and that it departs from the earlier PPP model of negotiating a specific mechanism during LCP.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary PPP decides during link setup which check to use. EAP does not, so the server can ask the first question and learn what the other end supports before choosing. That also lets a simple device forward the whole conversation to a server that does the real checking; it only needs to notice the final success or failure.

sections.title: The EAP Packet Format
sections.content:
Exactly one PPP EAP packet is encapsulated in the Information field of a PPP Data Link Layer frame where the protocol field indicates type hex C227, PPP EAP. The packet has four fields. The Code field is one octet and identifies the type of EAP packet: 1 Request, 2 Response, 3 Success and 4 Failure. The Identifier field is one octet and aids in matching responses with requests. The Length field is two octets and gives the length of the packet including the Code, Identifier, Length and Data fields, with octets outside that range treated as Data Link Layer padding and ignored on reception. The Data field is zero or more octets, and its format is determined by the Code field.

To negotiate EAP itself, the Authentication-Protocol Configuration Option is used. It is a Type field of 3, a Length field of 4, and an Authentication-Protocol field holding C227 in hex for the PPP Extensible Authentication Protocol.

A Request or Response packet adds two more fields. The Type field is one octet and indicates the type of the Request or Response, and only one Type may be specified per packet. Normally the Type of the Response is the same as that of the Request, but there is also a Nak Response Type for indicating that a Request type is unacceptable to the peer. When sending a Nak, the peer MAY indicate an alternative desired authentication Type which it supports. The Type-Data field varies with the Type of the Request and the associated Response.
sections.plainLanguage: Every EAP packet starts with three small fields: a one-octet code saying whether it is a request, a response, a success or a failure, a one-octet identifier used to pair a request with its answer, and a two-octet length. A request or a response then adds a one-octet type saying which check is being used, plus data that depends on that type.

sections.title: Requests, Responses and Retries
sections.content:
The Request packet is sent by the authenticator to the peer. The authenticator MUST transmit an EAP packet with the Code field set to 1, and additional Request packets MUST be sent until a valid Response is received or an optional retry counter expires. Retransmitted Requests MUST be sent with the same Identifier value so that they can be told apart from new Requests. The peer MUST send a Response in reply to a Request, and Responses MUST only be sent in reply to a received Request and never retransmitted on a timer. The Identifier of the Response MUST match that of the Request.

Because the authentication process will often involve user input, care must be taken over retransmission strategies and timeouts. The RFC suggests a retransmission timer of 6 seconds with a maximum of 10 retransmissions as the default, and notes that these timeouts may need to be longer in some cases, such as where token cards are involved. The peer must be prepared to silently discard received retransmissions while waiting for user input.

The Identifier rules follow from that. If a Request packet is retransmitted due to a timeout while waiting for a Response, the Identifier MUST be the same, and any new Request MUST modify it. If a peer receives a duplicate Request for which it has already sent a Response, it MUST resend that Response. If a peer receives a duplicate Request before it has sent a Response, meaning it is waiting for user input, it MUST silently discard the duplicate.

The Success packet is sent by the authenticator to acknowledge successful authentication, with the Code field set to 3. If the authenticator cannot authenticate the peer, because of unacceptable Responses to one or more Requests, it MUST transmit a packet with the Code field set to 4, Failure. An authenticator MAY issue multiple Requests before sending a Failure response in order to allow for human typing mistakes. Because Success and Failure are not acknowledged, they may be lost, and the peer MUST allow for that: a Network Protocol packet can serve as an alternative indication of Success, and the receipt of an LCP Terminate-Request can be taken as a Failure.
sections.plainLanguage: The server asks, the other end answers, and the server repeats until it has enough to decide, then sends success or failure. Because a person may be typing, the RFC suggests waiting six seconds before repeating a question and giving up after ten tries, and it says the other end should quietly drop a repeat of a question it is already answering.

sections.title: The Initial Request and Response Types
sections.content:
The initial set of EAP Types used in Request and Response exchanges is defined in this section, with more Types to come in follow-on documents. The Type field is one octet and identifies the structure of the packet. The first three Types are special cases, and the remaining Types define authentication exchanges. The Nak Type is valid only for Response packets and MUST NOT be sent in a Request; it must only be sent in response to a Request that uses an authentication Type code. All EAP implementations MUST support Types 1 to 4, and Types 5 and 6 are also defined here.

Identity, type 1, queries the identity of the peer. Generally the authenticator issues this as the initial Request, and an optional displayable message MAY be included to prompt the peer where interaction with a user is expected. A Response MUST be sent with a Type of 1, and its Type-Data returns the identity, zero bytes long if the identity is unknown. The field MUST NOT be null terminated. The RFC suggests retrying the Identity Request on an invalid identity or authentication failure to allow for typos, and suggests retrying it a minimum of 3 times before terminating the authentication phase with a Failure reply.

Notification, type 2, is optionally used to convey a displayable message from the authenticator to the peer, which the peer SHOULD display or log. It is intended for an acknowledged notification of some imperative nature, such as a password about to expire, an OTP sequence integer nearing 0, or an authentication failure warning. A Response MUST be sent with a Type field of 2 and a Type-Data field of zero octets.

Nak, type 3, is valid only in Response messages and is sent where the desired authentication Type is unacceptable. Authentication Types are numbered 4 and above, and the Response contains the authentication Type desired by the peer in a single octet.

MD5-Challenge, type 4, is analogous to the PPP CHAP protocol with MD5 as the specified algorithm. The Request contains a challenge and the Response MUST be of type 4 or type 3, where the Nak reply indicates the peer's desired mechanism. All EAP implementations MUST support this mechanism.

One-Time Password, type 5, follows the one-time password system defined in RFC 1938. The Request contains a displayable message holding an OTP challenge, and the Response must be of type 5 or type 3. The Response field carries the six words from the OTP dictionary. Generic Token Card, type 6, is defined for use with token card implementations that require user input: the Request contains an ASCII text message and the Reply contains the token card information needed for authentication, typically read by a user from the card and entered as ASCII text.
sections.plainLanguage: Six kinds of exchange are defined. Identity asks who is calling. Notification sends a message the other end must acknowledge, such as a warning that a password is about to expire. Nak says the question asked is not acceptable and names one that would be. MD5-Challenge is a challenge and answer based on the password, the same idea as CHAP. One-Time Password uses a code from a list. Generic Token Card reads the number off a small security token.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security issues are the primary topic of this RFC. The interaction of the authentication protocols within PPP is highly implementation dependent. For example, on failure of authentication some implementations do not terminate the link; instead the implementation limits the kind of traffic in the Network-Layer Protocols to a filtered subset, which allows the user an opportunity to update secrets or send mail to the network administrator indicating a problem.

There is no provision for retries of failed authentication, but the LCP state machine can renegotiate the authentication protocol at any time, thus allowing a new attempt. The RFC recommends that any counters used for authentication failure not be reset until after successful authentication, or subsequent termination of the failed link. There is no requirement that authentication be full duplex or that the same protocol be used in both directions, and it is perfectly acceptable for different protocols to be used in each direction.

The RFC warns that within or associated with each PPP server it is not anticipated that a particular named user would be authenticated by multiple methods, because that would make the user vulnerable to attacks which negotiate the least secure method from among a set, such as PAP rather than EAP. Instead, for each named user there should be an indication of exactly one method used to authenticate that user name. If a user needs different authentication methods under different circumstances, distinct identities SHOULD be employed.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC closes with a warning about mixing methods. If one user name can be checked by more than one mechanism, an attacker simply picks the weakest one. So each user name should have exactly one method, and a user who needs a second method should get a second identity.

items.label: Request
items.desc: Sent by the authenticator to ask the peer for something.

items.label: Response
items.desc: Sent by the peer in reply to a Request, with the same identifier.

items.label: Success
items.desc: Sent by the authenticator to end the phase with a pass.

items.label: Failure
items.desc: Sent by the authenticator to end the phase with a fail.

messages.label: REQUEST IDENTITY
messages.note: The authenticator asks who is calling.

messages.label: RESPONSE MD5-CHALLENGE
messages.note: The peer answers with the MD5 hash of the password and the challenge, or with a Nak naming a type it prefers.

messages.label: SUCCESS
messages.note: Or a Failure packet if the peer cannot be authenticated.

viz.caption: THE EAP REQUEST AND RESPONSE TYPES

items.label: Identity
items.desc: Asks the peer for its identity.

items.label: Notification
items.desc: An acknowledged message from the authenticator, such as a warning.

items.label: Nak
items.desc: Response only. The requested type is unacceptable; names the type the peer wants.

items.label: MD5-Challenge
items.desc: A challenge and answer based on the password, as in CHAP.

items.label: One-Time Password
items.desc: Uses a one-time code, as defined in RFC 1938.

items.label: Generic Token Card
items.desc: Carries information read from a token card.
